key_results: A recursive filter computes each output sample from present and past input samples plus previously computed output samples; the feedforward a coefficients and feedback b coefficients together define the recursion. Reusing output samples produces a long, usually exponentially decaying impulse response with only a few arithmetic operations. [Chapter 19, The Recursive Method, Eq. 19-1 and Table 19-1]

Recursive filters are called IIR because their ideal impulse responses continue indefinitely, whereas convolution filters are FIR. Smith's practical rule is that the IIR response can usually be truncated after roughly 15-20 time constants, once it falls below single-precision round-off noise. [Chapter 19, The Recursive Method; Phase Response, pp. 320, 325, and 332]

For a one-pole low-pass filter, a0 = 1-x and b1 = x; for the corresponding high-pass filter, a0 = (1+x)/2, a1 = -(1+x)/2, and b1 = x. The parameter 0<x<1 is the sample-to-sample decay. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Eqs. 19-2 and 19-3]

The one-pole decay parameter can be selected from a time constant d in samples by x = exp(-1/d), or from normalized -3 dB cutoff frequency fc by x = exp(-2πfc). This makes the digital filter directly analogous to an RC network. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Eqs. 19-4 and 19-5]

Cascading four one-pole low-pass stages improves stopband attenuation and retains fast execution, but the roll-off is still poor compared with a true frequency-selective filter. Smith supplies the combined coefficients a0=(1-x)^4 and b1=4x, b2=-6x^2, b3=4x^3, b4=-x^4. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Fig. 19-5 and Eq. 19-6]

Second-order band-pass and band-reject filters are parameterized by normalized center frequency f and bandwidth BW through R=1-3BW and a gain term K. They are effective for tones such as 60 Hz interference, but single precision limits the narrowest useful bandwidth to about 0.0003 of the sampling frequency. [Chapter 19, Narrow-band Filters, Eqs. 19-7 and 19-8 and Fig. 19-6]

Zero-phase impulse responses are symmetric about sample zero; linear-phase responses are shifted symmetric responses; asymmetric impulse responses have nonlinear phase and distort the two edges of a pulse differently. FIR symmetry makes exact linear phase easy, while causal IIR responses are inherently asymmetric. [Chapter 19, Phase Response, Fig. 19-7]

Any recursive filter can be made zero phase off-line by filtering forward and then backward. The phase cancels, the magnitude response is squared, and execution time approximately doubles; streamed blocks require overlap-add and padding on both sides. [Chapter 19, Phase Response, Eq. 19-9 and Fig. 19-8]

Integer IIR implementations face both coefficient representation and accumulated round-off/instability problems. Smith suggests rational coefficients or lookup tables, but recommends checking whether the recursive moving average can meet the requirement first because it is naturally integer-friendly. [Chapter 19, Using Integers]

A type-I Chebyshev response buys a faster transition by allowing passband ripple; setting ripple to zero gives the maximally flat Butterworth response. Smith recommends 0.5% ripple as a practical compromise and notes that elliptic filters achieve still faster roll-off by allowing ripple in both bands. [Chapter 20, The Chebyshev and Butterworth Responses, Fig. 20-1]

Chebyshev design in this chapter is determined by four choices: low-pass or high-pass, normalized cutoff, percent passband ripple, and an even number of poles. Cutoff is measured at amplitude 0.707 (-3 dB); more poles sharpen the transition, and filters near normalized 0 or 0.5 roll off faster for a given pole count. [Chapter 20, Designing the Filter, Fig. 20-2]

The cookbook design constructs complex-conjugate pole pairs, warps the Butterworth circle into a Chebyshev ellipse when ripple is nonzero, maps from the s-domain to the z-domain, transforms low-pass to low- or high-pass, combines stages, and normalizes gain. [Chapter 20, Designing the Filter, Tables 20-4 and 20-5]

Frequency-domain optimization costs time-domain behavior: Chebyshev step-response overshoot is about 5%-30%, depending mainly on pole count and somewhat on cutoff frequency. [Chapter 20, Step Response Overshoot, Fig. 20-3]

Round-off noise limits the safe pole count, especially near normalized cutoff 0 or 0.5. Smith's single-precision guide allows approximately 4 poles at 0.02/0.48, 6 at 0.05/0.45, 10 at 0.10/0.40, and 20 at 0.25. [Chapter 20, Stability, Table 20-3]

Higher-order recursive filters are made more stable by double precision or, preferably, by retaining the cascade of second-order sections instead of combining all pole pairs into one high-order recursion. [Chapter 20, Stability, Tables 20-4 through 20-6]

For comparable low-pass jobs, digital filters can be much flatter, steeper, and more linear-phase than analog filters; analog filters retain advantages in speed, very wide dynamic range, simplicity, and operation before sampling or after reconstruction. [Chapter 21, Match #1: Analog vs. Digital Filters, Fig. 21-1]

At moderate specifications a windowed-sinc FIR and Chebyshev IIR can both work. At extreme specifications the FIR can be extended to nearly arbitrary attenuation while the IIR reaches numerical/performance limits; the IIR is commonly about an order of magnitude faster at comparable performance. [Chapter 21, Match #2: Windowed-Sinc vs. Chebyshev, Figs. 21-2 through 21-5]

For time-domain smoothing, a moving average gives the fastest straight-line step transition, while a bidirectional one-pole filter gives a smoother rounded transition. The choice often turns on implementation: floating-point one-off work favors the easy recursive filter, while highly optimized integer products favor the moving average. [Chapter 21, Match #3: Moving Average vs. Single Pole, Figs. 21-6 and 21-7]

The cochlea's basilar membrane implements place coding: stiffness varies along its length so different locations respond to different frequencies. Neural firing also implements volley coding below roughly 4 kHz, with individual neurons limited to about 500 action potentials per second. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing, Fig. 22-1]

Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz-20 kHz and about 120 dB in intensity, yet resolves only about 120 loudness steps. Sensitivity peaks around 1-4 kHz; binaural direction uses head shadow above about 1 kHz and interaural delay below it. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing, Table 22-1]

Timbre is governed by harmonic amplitudes, not a unique waveform. Signals with identical component magnitudes but different relative phases normally sound the same because environmental propagation randomizes phase; one timbre can therefore correspond to infinitely many waveforms. [Chapter 22, Timbre, Figs. 22-2 and 22-3]

Audio information is approximately logarithmic in frequency. Each octave carries comparable perceptual information, explaining why telephone speech can retain intelligibility over 200 Hz-3.2 kHz even though it discards most of the linear 20 kHz bandwidth. [Chapter 22, Timbre; Sound Quality vs. Data Rate, Fig. 22-4]

Smith's reference data rates are 706 kbit/s for mono 44.1 kHz, 16-bit high-fidelity audio; 96 kbit/s for 8 kHz, 12-bit telephone speech; 64 kbit/s after 8-bit companding; and about 4 kbit/s for LPC-compressed speech. [Chapter 22, Sound Quality vs. Data Rate, Table 22-2]

CD playback expands 8 data bits to 14 by EFM to control pit run lengths, uses Reed-Solomon redundancy for correction/concealment, recovers 16-bit 44.1 kHz samples, and commonly interpolates by four before a simpler analog reconstruction filter. [Chapter 22, High Fidelity Audio, Figs. 22-5 and 22-6]

Companding matches quantization steps to logarithmic hearing: telephone-quality speech can use 8 unequal bits instead of 12 uniform bits. North American μ255 law and European A-law are nearly identical except near zero; their mappings are given explicitly. [Chapter 22, Companding, Eqs. 22-1 and 22-2 and Fig. 22-7]

Voiced speech consists of quasi-periodic vocal-cord excitation shaped by resonances of the vocal tract; fricatives are noise-like. Spectrograms expose changing formants, while recognition remains harder than matching isolated acoustic patterns because human listeners exploit context and expectations. [Chapter 22, Speech Synthesis and Recognition, Figs. 22-8 and 22-9]

Wideband speech noise can be reduced by short-time, time-varying spectral weighting: large spectral components are treated as signal, small ones as noise, and overlapping windowed frames are recombined smoothly. [Chapter 22, Nonlinear Audio Processing, Fig. 22-10]

Homomorphic processing linearizes multiplicative mixtures with a logarithm and convolutional mixtures with Fourier transform followed by logarithm. Linear filtering can then separate components before the transforms are inverted, but nonlinearities create aliasing and overlapping harmonics that may defeat separation. [Chapter 22, Nonlinear Audio Processing, Figs. 22-11 and 22-12]

A digital image is a two-dimensional array of pixels whose values encode a physical parameter. Smith treats the spatial domain as primary: image information is carried mainly by edges and regions, not sinusoids. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure, Fig. 23-1]

Sample spacing and sampling aperture are independent: the grid says where measurements are taken, while the aperture says what surrounding region contributes to each pixel. Final resolution is limited by the worse of the two. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure, Fig. 23-1]

Eight-bit grayscale is usually adequate for display because 1/256 brightness steps are below visual discrimination and spatial dithering averages neighboring values, though scientific acquisition may need more bits to preserve nonvisual information. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure]

Cameras and eyes share a lens, adjustable aperture, and sensor, but the eye achieves most of its huge dynamic range by adapting receptor sensitivity rather than by pupil area alone. Reflection images can be modeled as reflectance multiplied by illumination, motivating later illumination flattening. [Chapter 23, Cameras and Eyes, Figs. 23-2 through 23-6]

Brightness adds an offset to every pixel; contrast changes the slope around a chosen midpoint. Both are point operations implementable by a 256-entry lookup table, with clipping when transformed values exceed the display range. [Chapter 23, Brightness and Contrast Adjustments, Figs. 23-10 through 23-12]

A grayscale transform allocates output contrast according to the slope of its lookup curve. A desired contrast weighting is integrated and normalized to construct the transform; histogram equalization automates this by integrating the image histogram and maximizes entropy, but can neglect semantically important rare pixels. [Chapter 23, Grayscale Transforms, Figs. 23-13 and 23-14]

Warping computes, for each destination pixel, a comes-from address in the source. Nearest-neighbor sampling is simple but jagged; bilinear interpolation combines the four surrounding source pixels and gives the same result regardless of whether horizontal or vertical interpolation is performed first. [Chapter 23, Warping, Figs. 23-15 and 23-16]

Two-dimensional convolution carries over the impulse-response view: the image impulse response is the point spread function (PSF), and every input pixel contributes a scaled, shifted PSF to the output. In the output-side view, the PSF is flipped horizontally and vertically. [Chapter 24, Convolution; A Closer Look at Image Convolution, Eq. 24-3 and Figs. 24-14 and 24-15]

Common smoothing PSFs are pillbox, Gaussian, and square kernels; edge enhancement follows spectral inversion by negating a smoothing kernel and adding a centered impulse. Retinal lateral inhibition is a biological edge enhancer and creates Mach bands. [Chapter 24, Convolution, Figs. 24-1 through 24-3]

A 3x3 PSF is enough for many edge operations, including gradient-like edge detection and sharpening, because it reaches immediate neighbors while requiring only nine multiply-accumulates per output pixel. [Chapter 24, 3x3 Edge Modification, Fig. 24-4]

A PSF is separable when h[r,c]=vert[r]horz[c]. Convolving rows and then columns reduces work for an N by N image and M by M kernel from proportional to N²M² to N²M; the Gaussian is the only circularly symmetric separable PSF. [Chapter 24, Convolution by Separability, Eq. 24-1 and Figs. 24-5 through 24-7]

Rectangular and double-sided-exponential separable kernels can be implemented recursively, making cost proportional to N² and independent of PSF width; repeated applications approach a Gaussian by the central limit theorem. [Chapter 24, Convolution by Separability]

Uneven illumination can be estimated with a very broad smoothing PSF. Subtracting that estimate approximates reflectance linearly, while dividing the viewed image by the illumination estimate better matches the multiplicative formation model but is nonlinear. [Chapter 24, Example of a Large PSF: Illumination Flattening, Fig. 24-8]

A two-dimensional DFT is computed by applying one-dimensional FFTs to every row and then every column (or vice versa). Typical image spectra look unintuitive because the source information is spatial; Fourier analysis is most useful for convolution/deconvolution and projection relationships. [Chapter 24, Fourier Image Analysis, Figs. 24-9 and 24-10 and Eq. 24-2]

FFT correlation zero-pads image and target to contain the full linear convolution, transforms both, multiplies complex spectra, and inverse-transforms. Edge-filtering the target sharpens the correlation peak, but exact target size and orientation remain critical. [Chapter 24, FFT Convolution, Figs. 24-11 through 24-13]

Conventional image convolution costs O(N²M²); FFT convolution costs approximately O(N² log N). In Smith's example, FFT becomes worthwhile around a 10x10 kernel versus floating-point direct convolution, or around 30x30 versus integer direct convolution. [Chapter 24, A Closer Look at Image Convolution, Fig. 24-16]

Spatial resolution can be described by PSF full-width at half maximum, MTF limiting frequency, line-spread width, or 10%-90% edge-response distance. Smith favors edge response because it matches how image information is encoded, is easy to acquire, and converts to MTF through first difference plus a one-dimensional FFT. [Chapter 25, Spatial Resolution, Figs. 25-1 through 25-5]

Resolution is aperture-limited when more than about three samples span a 10%-90% edge, spacing-limited when fewer than one sample spans it, and jointly limited between one and three samples. A sufficiently broad aperture acts as an antialias filter. [Chapter 25, Sample Spacing and Sampling Aperture, Fig. 25-6]

Detectability depends on object contrast divided by noise standard deviation and begins to fail around SNR=1. Smoothing with a kernel matched to object size improves SNR by the square root of the number of averaged pixels, so detectability scales with the square root of object area. [Chapter 25, Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Figs. 25-7 and 25-8]

Counting (Poisson) noise has standard deviation equal to the square root of the mean count, hence SNR equal to the square root of the count. Improving SNR by a factor of two therefore requires four times as many photons, x-rays, or electrons. [Chapter 25, Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Eq. 25-1 and Fig. 25-9]

Binary morphology uses erosion to shrink/break objects, dilation to expand/merge them, opening (erosion then dilation) to remove small object islands and thin protrusions, and closing (dilation then erosion) to fill small holes and gaps. [Chapter 25, Morphological Image Processing, Fig. 25-10]

Skeletonization iteratively removes boundary pixels while preserving endpoints and connectivity; Smith's implementation marks removable pixels first and deletes them only after scanning the whole image to avoid directional bias. [Chapter 25, Morphological Image Processing, Figs. 25-11 and 25-12 and Tables 25-1 and 25-2]

Each CT view sample is a line integral through the slice. Filtered backprojection filters every view before smearing it back along its acquisition rays, exactly reconstructing the ideal image in the limit of infinitely many samples and views. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-14 through 25-17]

The Fourier slice theorem states that the one-dimensional spectrum of a projection is a radial slice through the two-dimensional image spectrum at the same angle. Backprojection's radial sampling density varies as 1/f, so the correction filter has magnitude proportional to f, with the kernel specified by Eq. 25-2. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-18 and 25-19 and Eq. 25-2]

Target and nontarget distributions must be combined with prevalence/base rates when turning a test value into probability. Ignoring a rare target's prior probability can change a seemingly 25% posterior to 0.025% in Smith's cancer-test example. [Chapter 26, Target Detection, Fig. 26-1]

Threshold choice trades false positives against false negatives. An ROC curve plots target-positive rate against nontarget-positive rate across thresholds; better systems bend toward the upper-left, while random guessing follows the diagonal. [Chapter 26, Target Detection, Figs. 26-2 through 26-4]

Smith's standard neural network is fully connected input-hidden-output: passive input nodes fan out, active nodes form weighted sums, and a sigmoid maps each sum to 0-1. A bias input of one shifts sigmoid thresholds. [Chapter 26, Neural Network Architecture, Figs. 26-5 through 26-7, Eqs. 26-1 and 26-2]

The hidden layer can be interpreted as a bank of correlators followed by smooth probability-like thresholds, and the output layer as a correlation of correlations—a detector of patterns of patterns. The nonlinearity is essential; without it, adjacent linear layers collapse into one. [Chapter 26, Neural Network Architecture; Why Does It Work?]

Training is optimization over examples, not derivation of human-readable rules. Smith's vowel detector uses 100 pixels plus a bias, 10 hidden nodes, one output, and 1,020 learned weights, with separate training and test images. [Chapter 26, Training the Neural Network, Fig. 26-8 and Tables 26-2 and 26-3]

Steepest descent updates each weight in proportion to output sensitivity, current example error, and step size μ. Backpropagated slopes use the sigmoid derivative s'(x)=s(x)(1-s(x)); too large μ oscillates/diverges and too small μ converges slowly. [Chapter 26, Training the Neural Network, Eqs. 26-3 through 26-5 and Fig. 26-9]

Network quality must be measured on held-out examples and across thresholds, not only by training error. In Smith's best trial, a point on the ROC curve detects 96% of vowels with 4% false positives; random initialization causes materially different solutions. [Chapter 26, Evaluating the Results, Figs. 26-10 through 26-12]

Custom IIR magnitude responses can be designed by finite-difference steepest descent on recursion coefficients: impulse-response FFT gives the current magnitude, RMS spectral error defines the objective, and μ is reduced when a step worsens error. Initial coefficients must describe a stable system. [Chapter 26, Recursive Filter Design, Tables 26-4 and 26-5 and Fig. 26-13]
pedagogy: These eight chapters preserve Smith's intuition-first, tool-building style while moving from core filter mechanics into applications. Every difficult abstraction is attached to a physical or visual model: an absent-minded professor motivates feedback recursion; RC circuits explain one-pole filters; filters compete in staged 'matches'; the ear becomes a spectrum analyzer; image formation becomes illumination multiplied by reflectance; retinal inhibition becomes a PSF; CT becomes rays, smearing, and spokes; and steepest descent becomes a paratrooper walking downhill in fog. Formal proofs are largely omitted. Instead, compact equations, plots, exact numerical design tables, BASIC-like programs, debug data, and before/after image sequences make algorithms executable. Chapters 19-21 assume prior convolution, FFT, and basic filter concepts; Chapters 22-25 assume elementary acoustics, sampling, probability, and image arrays; Chapter 26 assumes the shard's earlier correlation, histograms, and iterative-filter ideas. Complex-number machinery and z-transform derivations are intentionally deferred. There are no conventional end-of-chapter exercises. Worked comparisons, parameter sweeps, debugging tables, full programs, visual experiments, and design warnings function as exercises-by-inspection. Several implementation timings and speech-recognition expectations are historically dated, but the conceptual tradeoffs, failure modes, and experimental habits remain pedagogically strong.

gems: The vanished-professor story asks what information remained available to calculate y[28], making feedback recursion feel inevitable rather than formal. [Chapter 19, The Recursive Method, Fig. 19-1]

A one-pole filter with x=0.86 has a 6.63-sample time constant; the number turns an abstract feedback coefficient into visible exponential memory. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Eq. 19-4 and Fig. 19-3]

Forward-plus-reverse filtering earns Smith's theatrical 'Voila!' and a backwards warning sentence, a memorable reveal that exact zero phase costs only a second pass. [Chapter 19, Phase Response, Fig. 19-8]

Smith offers two definitions of a pole: roots of a complex denominator, or containers of magic powder—the more poles, the better the filter. The joke cleanly separates usage from derivation. [Chapter 20, Designing the Filter]

The unstable 6-pole, fc=0.01 coefficient set makes the numerical problem visceral: a coefficients near 10^-9 are overwhelmed by round-off in b coefficients near ten. [Chapter 20, Stability, Table 20-1]

The filter-comparison chapter stages three literal prize fights and reaches a crisp maxim: the windowed-sinc is a powerhouse, the Chebyshev is quick and agile. [Chapter 21, Match #2: Windowed-Sinc vs. Chebyshev]

A maximum-performance thought experiment asks for a 100 mV, 61 Hz signal riding on a 120 V, 60 Hz power line; the 1001-tap FIR crushes the 6-pole IIR if one can wait. [Chapter 21, Match #2: Windowed-Sinc vs. Chebyshev, Fig. 21-4]

The ear's dynamic range reaches roughly one million in amplitude, yet the eardrum moves less than a molecule's diameter at threshold and listeners perceive only about 120 loudness increments. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing, Table 22-1]
Covering 99% of a wall with perfect soundproofing still leaves perceived loudness near 20%, because loudness scales roughly as sound power to the one-third power. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing]

A 3-degree directional discrimination corresponds to roughly 30 microseconds of interaural delay for a 22 cm head—an arresting bridge from perception to sampling-scale timing. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing]
Two dramatically different 1 kHz ± 3 kHz waveforms sound the same, showing why waveform shape is not a one-to-one description of timbre. [Chapter 22, Timbre, Fig. 22-2]
The piano spans only about 20% of the linear 20 kHz hearing range but more than 70% of perceptual information because it covers seven of roughly ten audible octaves. [Chapter 22, Timbre, Fig. 22-4]

CD's physical story connects 0.8-3.5 μm pits, EFM's 8-to-14 mapping, Reed-Solomon protection, 4.3 Mbit/s raw storage, and 706 kbit/s recovered audio in one chain. [Chapter 22, High Fidelity Audio, Figs. 22-5 and 22-6]
The paired phrases 'spider ring' and 'spy during' illustrate why acoustic word matching without context is not speech understanding. [Chapter 22, Speech Synthesis and Recognition]
Homomorphic jargon literally swaps pieces of words—cepstrum, quefrency, liftering—because time and frequency roles have been reversed. [Chapter 22, Nonlinear Audio Processing, Fig. 22-12]
A 200x200 radar image of Venus is peeled into a 16x16 pixel patch and then into its exact numbers, making 'image as array' concrete. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure, Fig. 23-1]
One second of Smith-era digital audio is about 8 kB while one second of television is about 8 MB; a 1000x1000 image quadruples the burden of 500x500. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure]

The infrared intruder/truck example shows manual grayscale design making background and grille details visible at the explicit expense of the human body's contrast. [Chapter 23, Grayscale Transforms, Figs. 23-13 and 23-14]
Mach bands turn the retina's useful edge enhancement into an illusion: the dark side looks darker and the light side lighter near a gradual boundary. [Chapter 24, Convolution, Figs. 24-1 and 24-2]

A 512x512 image convolved with a 64x64 PSF needs more than a billion multiply-adds, motivating 3x3 kernels, separability, and FFT convolution as three distinct escape routes. [Chapter 24, Convolution]

The Gaussian is uniquely both circularly symmetric and separable; broad rectangular or exponential kernels can go further and make cost independent of kernel width. [Chapter 24, Convolution by Separability, Fig. 24-7]

A line-pair gauge slightly overstates resolution because its square-wave fundamental is 4/π ≈ 1.27 times the square-wave amplitude—an often ignored measurement wrinkle. [Chapter 25, Spatial Resolution, Fig. 25-2]

Doubling an object's diameter lets it be detected in roughly twice as much noise, because matched spatial averaging makes detectability scale with the square root of area. [Chapter 25, Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Fig. 25-8]

The 1972 EMI Mark I used ART, while filtered backprojection later became dominant; the chapter turns that history into a progression from iterative correction to exact DSP reconstruction. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-15 through 25-17]
The Fourier-slice 'wheel spokes are denser near the hub' analogy makes the ramp filter H(f)=|f| almost visually inevitable. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-18 and 25-19]

The rare-cancer example demonstrates base-rate neglect numerically: identical instrument output can suggest 25% disease probability or only 0.025% once prevalence is included. [Chapter 26, Target Detection, Fig. 26-1]

Smith's paratrooper dropped into a foggy mountain valley compares blind random evolution with measuring north/east slopes and walking downhill—the chapter's central steepest-descent analogy. [Chapter 26, Training the Neural Network, Fig. 26-9]

The best handwritten-vowel network detects 24 of 25 vowels with one false alarm per 25 nonvowels, despite hidden-layer weights that look like random noise to a person. [Chapter 26, Evaluating the Results, Figs. 26-10 through 26-12]

The same iterative machinery used to train a neural network designs a custom recursive filter, joining apparently different topics through the shared idea of optimizing many parameters. [Chapter 26, Recursive Filter Design, Fig. 26-13]
